body.text: Australia has developed a growing class of self-declared geopolitical analysts and independent researchers who built their reputations not through research, experience or sustained analytical work but through podcasts, social media feeds and confident commentary. Platforms such as X, YouTube and Substack have democratised debate. But they’ve also blurred the meaning of expertise.

Free speech allows anyone to express a view about politics, geopolitics or national security. That freedom sits at the heart of liberal democracy and should never be curtailed. But public debate suffers when authoritative terms such as ‘analyst’ and ‘researcher’ become branding tools used to legitimise opinion.

Across social media, a growing number of personalities describe themselves as political analysts, geopolitical analysts or independent researchers. Many have limited professional experience and no demonstrated record of research outputs. Yet their commentary increasingly circulates alongside work produced by think tanks, universities and professional analysts and is often treated as equivalent.

The problem isn’t confined to online personalities. In Australia’s political ecosystem, it’s now possible to find individuals presented as research directors despite having no academic qualifications or professional experience in their stated areas of expertise. When those individuals present themselves publicly as analysts or researchers, the title risks conveying a level of expertise that simply doesn’t exist.

Some will dismiss concerns like this as the complaints of an old man shouting at the clouds of technological change. They miss the point. This isn’t about nostalgia or putting analysts on a pedestal. It’s about truth in research and integrity in analysis.

Shoot-from-the-hip commentary appears daily from individuals presenting themselves as analysts or researchers without the training, experience or methodological grounding normally associated with those roles.
That distinction matters. Titles such as researcher and analyst have historically signalled method, experience and accountability.

A researcher investigates questions systematically to generate knowledge. An analyst interprets evidence to produce judgments. Australia doesn’t regulate these titles, but credible research and analysis rest on identifiable foundations: evidence, structured reasoning and accountability.
Experience matters as much as formal qualifications. What matters is whether claims are grounded in evidence and tested against reality.

Serious research institutions build systems to test whether knowledge claims are credible. Work is subject to peer review, editorial scrutiny and institutional oversight. Analysts develop expertise through years of practice, collecting evidence, testing assumptions and learning from error.

Social media operates differently. It rewards speed, certainty and emotional resonance over rigour. Audiences of video and audio content reward confidence rather than evidence. Algorithms amplify engagement, not expertise.
The result is an environment where polemic opinion frequently presents itself as analysis.

None of this means individuals without formal qualifications should remain silent. Open societies benefit from diverse perspectives. But when loose opinion adopts the language of expertise without transparency about its limits, policy debates risk becoming competitions of confidence rather than contests of evidence.

Reclaiming the meaning of authoritative terms requires only clarity, not censorship. Before accepting commentary presented as analysis, Australians should ask simple questions: How reliable is the information? Where does it come from? What experience does the author have? What evidence supports the claim?
People have every right to express their beliefs. But the confidence we place in those beliefs should depend on the credibility behind them.

When everyone becomes an analyst, the word stops meaning anything. Restoring its meaning will not silence debate. It will help Australians distinguish between evidence and opinion presented with confidence.
